analysis.one_liner: Strips EPA's power to regulate greenhouse gases from anything but vehicle tailpipes.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have taken the Supreme Court's 2007 ruling in Massachusetts v. EPA, which found that greenhouse gases are air pollutants under the Clean Air Act, and limited it to motor vehicles only. That would have stopped the EPA from using that ruling to write climate rules for power plants, factories, and other stationary sources of carbon emissions. The bill was a single-sponsor effort by Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming with no cosponsors; it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil, and gas producers and other carbon-intensive industries, including electric utilities and manufacturers that burn fossil fuels. The bill would have removed the legal foundation for EPA limits on their greenhouse gas emissions, avoiding compliance costs and leaving vehicle tailpipe rules as the only federal carbon standard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

how_it_helps.text: The bill limits the Supreme Court's Massachusetts v. EPA decision and the EPA's proposed endangerment finding on greenhouse gases to sources already regulated under Clean Air Act section 202, which covers new motor vehicles and engines [S2] [S3].

Because section 202 applies only to motor vehicles, the effect is to foreclose EPA greenhouse gas standards for power plants, refineries, and other stationary sources that rely on that ruling [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, who would lose a regulatory tool for limiting carbon pollution from power plants and heavy industry, the largest sources of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, and bear the health and climate costs that come with it.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the bill's approach argued in good faith that the Clean Air Act, written in 1970, was a poor and costly fit for controlling carbon dioxide, and that a sweeping regulatory program affecting power plants and manufacturing should be written by Congress rather than adopted by an agency under a court ruling.

Blocking stationary-source rules would have left tailpipe standards as the only federal greenhouse gas limits, allowing emissions from the largest U.S. sources, electric generation and heavy industry, to continue unchecked [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is real but narrow: fossil-fuel-dependent states and industries would avoid compliance costs, and there is a serious argument that Congress rather than the EPA should set climate policy. The cost is much larger: it would have removed the only available legal path to limiting carbon pollution from power plants and factories, the sources that dominate U.S. emissions, with no legislative replacement offered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never heard from again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY) introduced the bill on August 6, 2009 [S1] [S2].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
No cosponsors signed on, no further committee or floor action was ever recorded, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 without the bill advancing [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA's authority under Massachusetts v. EPA to regulate greenhouse gases from power plants and other industrial sources remained intact through the 111th Congress. The fossil fuel and utility interests that would have gained from blocking those rules did not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA climate authority survived; industry gains were blocked

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit the Massachusetts v. EPA ruling to motor vehicle sources.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so the bill's support level on either side of the aisle was never measured [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have removed the legal basis for EPA greenhouse gas limits on stationary sources, sparing fossil fuel producers and their customers in heavy industry from carbon regulation. The public would bear the resulting emissions and health costs.

Power plants and industrial facilities are the largest sources of greenhouse gases covered by the EPA rules the bill targets; blocking those rules would have spared them compliance costs. Some utilities that had already planned for carbon rules would have gained less than others.

The bill would have preserved vehicle emission standards under Clean Air Act section 2002 (section 202) as the sole federal greenhouse gas program, keeping tailpipe rules in place rather than deregulating them.
